stem: Which description best matches a log?

options.text: A timestamped message emitted by a service, not necessarily tied to a particular request
options.note: Right. That's how the OpenTelemetry primer defines a log.

options.text: A numeric aggregation over time, such as error rate
options.note: That describes a metric.

options.text: The path of one request through many services
options.note: That describes a trace.

options.text: A single unit of work within a request
options.note: That describes a span.

explanation: A log is a timestamped message emitted by services or other components. Unlike traces, logs aren't necessarily associated with any particular user request or transaction.
hint: Logs have the oldest history of the three signals.

stem: Which description best matches a metric?

options.text: An aggregation over a period of time of numeric data, such as request rate or CPU use
options.note: Right. That's the primer's definition.

options.text: A free-text line written for each request
options.note: That describes a log line.

options.text: A record of every function call
options.note: That's closer to profiling or detailed tracing.

options.text: A screenshot of a dashboard
options.note: A dashboard displays metrics. It isn't one.

explanation: Metrics are aggregations over a period of time of numeric data about your infrastructure or application, such as error rate, CPU utilisation and request rate.

sources.title: OpenTelemetry › Observability primer › Reliability and metrics

stem: How does OpenTelemetry describe the relationship between logs and events?

options.text: Events are a special type of log: all events are logs, but not all logs are events
options.note: Right. An event is a log record with an event name.

options.text: Events and logs are completely unrelated signals
options.note: In OpenTelemetry, events are a kind of log.

options.text: All logs are events, but not all events are logs
options.note: Reversed.

options.text: Events are a kind of metric
options.note: Events are modelled as log records.

explanation: Logs are anything you send through a Logging Provider, and events are a special type of log. Not all logs are events, but all events are logs.

stem: Which question is best answered with logs rather than metrics?

options.text: Exactly what happened to order #4711 when its payment failed at 14:02?
options.note: Right. Per-event detail is what logs keep.

options.text: Is the payment error rate higher than an hour ago?
options.note: That's a trend over many events, which is a metric question.

options.text: How many requests per second is the API serving?
options.note: That's a rate, a classic metric.

options.text: Should we page someone because errors exceed 5%?
options.note: Alerting on a ratio is a metric job.

explanation: Metrics aggregate numeric data over time. Logs record individual timestamped events with their details, useful for investigating specific incidents.
hint: One specific item, or a trend?

stem: What does the Prometheus FAQ say about feeding logs into Prometheus?

options.text: Don't. Use a log system such as Grafana Loki or OpenSearch
options.note: Right. Prometheus is a metrics system, not an event logging system.

options.text: Push them through the Pushgateway
options.note: The Pushgateway is for batch job metrics.

options.text: Store each line as a label value
options.note: That's unbounded cardinality, and still not a log store.

options.text: Use remote write to send logs in
options.note: Remote write carries samples, not logs.

explanation: Short answer: Don't! Use something like Grafana Loki or OpenSearch instead. Prometheus is a system to collect and process metrics, not an event logging system.
hint: The FAQ answer is one word.

sources.title: Prometheus FAQ › How to feed logs into Prometheus?

stem: How do the Prometheus docs suggest connecting logging and metrics in your code?

options.text: Increment a counter for every line of logging code
options.note: Right. Then you can see how often a message is happening.

options.text: Expose each log message as a metric label
options.note: That's unbounded cardinality.

options.text: Replace logging entirely with metrics
options.note: Logs are still valuable for detail.

options.text: Log every metric value once a second
options.note: That's backwards and wasteful.

explanation: As a general rule, for every line of logging code you should also have a counter that is incremented. Totals of info, error and warning lines are also useful.

stem: A developer proposes a metric with a request_id label so each request is visible in Prometheus. What's the problem?

options.text: Unbounded label values explode cardinality. Per-request detail belongs in logs or traces
options.note: Right. Count requests in a metric and keep the IDs elsewhere.

options.text: Prometheus labels can't contain dashes
options.note: Label values can contain any UTF-8 characters.

options.text: Request IDs must be stored as gauges
options.note: The type isn't the issue. Cardinality is.

options.text: There's no problem. That's best practice
options.note: It's a classic anti-pattern.

explanation: Every unique label combination is a new series. Avoid unbounded values such as user IDs. Prometheus isn't an event logging system, so per-event detail goes to logs.

sources.title: Prometheus FAQ › How to feed logs into Prometheus?

stem: Why are structured logs preferred in production?

options.text: Their consistent schema makes them easy to parse, validate and correlate with traces and metrics
options.note: Right. OpenTelemetry recommends them for production.

options.text: They're always smaller than unstructured logs
options.note: Size isn't the reason given.

options.text: Prometheus can scrape them directly
options.note: Prometheus doesn't ingest logs.

options.text: Any JSON log is automatically structured
options.note: The docs warn JSON alone may only be semistructured without a stable schema.

explanation: Structured logs are preferred in production because their stable schema makes them straightforward to validate, parse, correlate with traces and metrics, and analyse at scale.

stem: Which are the three main telemetry signals described in the OpenTelemetry primer? Select all that apply.

options.text: Metrics
options.note: Right. Aggregated numeric data over time.

options.text: Logs
options.note: Right. Timestamped records of what happened.

options.text: Traces
options.note: Right. The path of a request through services.

options.text: Dashboards
options.note: Dashboards display telemetry. They aren't a signal.

explanation: Telemetry is data emitted from a system and its behaviour. It can come in the form of traces, metrics and logs.
hint: Data the system emits, not ways to view it.

sources.title: OpenTelemetry › Observability primer › Reliability and metrics

stem: What makes logs much more useful for tracking code execution across a request?

options.text: Including them in, or correlating them with, a trace and span
options.note: Right. The primer says logs lack context on their own.

options.text: Writing them in upper case
options.note: Formatting doesn't add context.

options.text: Storing them in Prometheus
options.note: Prometheus doesn't store logs.

options.text: Removing timestamps
options.note: Timestamps are essential.

explanation: Logs aren't enough for tracking code execution, as they usually lack context such as where they were called from. They become far more useful as part of a span, or correlated with a trace and span.
hint: This leads into the next topic.
